text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- Major pension funds say they were misled by Den Danske Bank in the purchase of shares in Hafnia insurance company before its collapse but the funds themselves were well-informed as to events inside Hafnia and will have a hard time making a case.

-- Lego's results, published on Monday, show that although business is improving for the toymaker it is not good enough. The group's sales rose by four percent in 1996 compared to the previous year and it declared a pre-tax profit of 699 million crowns.

-- The Danish Burma Committee, a lobby group supporting Burmese pro-democracy campaigners, is renewing pressure on businesses trading in Burma, particularly FLS, Ericsson and Hydro Texaco. The committee is launch a petition on May 1 calling on business leaders to pay fresh attention to the Burmese military government's civil rights record.

-- Travel managers in 42 of Denmark's biggest companies want the EU to limit or ban airline bonus schemes, arguing that they hinder competition and encourage business travellers to seek bonus points when making a booking, rather than the most cost-effective deal.

-- House prices are rising in tandem with the falling current account deficit, because Danes are no longer putting their savings into their properties but instead using their capital for consumption, says a lecturer at Copenhagen business school, blaming the growing number of schemes and instruments for refinancing property.

-- Copenhagen's city council plans to build a fibre-optic cable network, access to which it will rent to new operators in the recently deregulated telecoms sector. Local authorities in Sweden have shown that the undertaking can be profitable and Copenhagen's Lord Mayor Jens Kramer Mikkelsen promises clients lower prices and better service than former monopoly Tel Danmark.
